entry.title: Movity Video Platform Launched – A Vimeo Alternative with Frame-Level Search, H.265 4K Streaming, AI-Made Work Excluded
entry.summary: Movity is a new video hosting and portfolio platform for filmmakers, built by cinematographer and director Arkadiy Kreslov. It combines hosting, client review, and embeds with a search engine that finds films by their key frames, color palette, and dialogue. A curated public feed
entry.content:
Movity is a new video hosting and portfolio platform for filmmakers, built by cinematographer and director Arkadiy Kreslov. It combines hosting, client review, and embeds with a search engine that finds films by their key frames, color palette, and dialogue. A curated public feed accepts only verified filmmakers and excludes work made primarily with generative AI. Let’s take a closer look.

We’ve written and spoken about Vimeo quite a bit lately. Bending Spoons acquired the platform in late 2025, and in January 2026 we reported that Vimeo layoffs eliminated the majority of staff just four months after the deal. We also looked at how Vimeo betrayed the filmmakers who built it, as well as an opinion piece by my colleague Jeff Loch on how Vimeo is holding him hostage. We also covered Bending Spoons’ Nasdaq IPO in July.

Other filmmakers have started building alternatives, such as rushes.cc, a European alternative to Vimeo that we covered in March. Movity enters the same space, with a stronger focus on discovery and on keeping AI-generated work out of its public feed.

Movity positions itself as a direct alternative to Vimeo. According to the company, the platform streams in H.265 at up to three times Vimeo’s bitrate, with up to 4K on the Pro plan and an H.264 fallback for playback on all devices. Filmmakers can upload ProRes masters directly, along with most other major formats, so there is no need to export a separate delivery file first. A transfer wizard moves an existing Vimeo library at source quality. Movity streams through a global network in more than 330 cities, which the company says helps playback start quickly wherever the viewer is.

Built by a working cinematographer

Arkadiy Kreslov has more than 16 years of experience as a cinematographer and director on high-end productions. He studied cinematography at the Filmakademie Baden-Württemberg in Germany, directed and shot for German rapper, songwriter, and musician Peter Fox, and has worked with brands such as Nike, Timberland, and Porsche, as well as with artists such as Robin Schulz and Rita Ora. He also worked as a video commissioner for Warner Music Central Europe. According to the company, Kreslov started coding at 12, sold his first commercial software at 14, and was mentored as a young programmer by Joseph Weizenbaum, who built ELIZA, the first chatbot, and later became one of the most prominent critics of AI.

You saw a scene in a great ad years ago – the light, the mood – and now you need it. So you scroll through your Vimeo likes, guessing from thumbnails and titles. Or you dig through Instagram and festival sites, because you can only find a film if you remember its name or who made it. On Movity, you search for what’s in the image, and you find it.

Kreslov describing the problem Movity is meant to solve

Search by frame, color, and dialogue

Search is the core of the platform. When a filmmaker uploads a video, Movity extracts key frames automatically, and the filmmaker selects which frames represent the work. The platform reads the color palette of each selected frame, so users can find films by color. A machine learning model analyzes only these selected frames, not the full video, and makes them searchable by natural language and visual similarity. Users can describe a scene, a mood, or the way light falls on a face, or select a palette, and get matching films.

Speech is transcribed automatically, so dialogue is searchable too, and the transcript can be turned into subtitles with one click. Subtitles can also be translated into other languages for festivals and international clients. Users can collect frames and films into boards, similar to a moodboard. The free plan includes 60 frames per month; Creator includes 500; and Pro includes 1,500.

Movity states that machine learning on the platform only serves to understand footage and speech, never to generate content, and that the company does not train AI on users’ work.

Two sides: a hosting tool and a curated feed

Movity works on two levels. Any filmmaker can use it as a video platform from day one for hosting, sharing, client review, embeds, and search across their own library. On top of that sits the public feed, which is curated. Only verified filmmakers can publish there; every creator is reviewed by a person, and work made primarily with generative AI is not allowed.

The Watch feed is a reels-style, ad-free stream of films, personalized for each viewer. According to the company, recommendations stay focused on filmmaking, rather than drifting to content about a music video’s song as they often do on YouTube. Movity Selects gives standout films their own page with key frames, color palette, a director’s note, and behind-the-scenes photos from set.

Each upload has a credit section with role templates for short films and other formats, plus custom roles. Crew members are tagged with an @mention, so the film also appears on their profiles, and full credit lists can be pasted in one go. Filmmakers can also tag the camera, lenses, and film stock from a database of hundreds of cameras, lens series, and stocks. Searching by gear, such as music videos shot on an ARRI 416 with ZEISS lenses, is still in development.

Client work and moving from Vimeo

For client work, Movity offers branded share links with passwords, expiry dates, and per-viewer analytics. Review tools include timeline comments, annotations, and approval workflows, and version stacks keep every cut of a film together, from v1 to final. A customizable embed player supports oEmbed, and a public player API is available for portfolio websites. Clips can also be trimmed and exported for Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and TikTok in a few clicks.

The platform also includes a transfer wizard for filmmakers moving from Vimeo. It connects to an existing Vimeo account and transfers the library at source quality. Users who switch to a yearly Pro plan get their remaining paid Vimeo time credited (up to three months), and Movity will swap up to 15 website embeds for free. The full library can be exported again at any time.

Movity also targets filmmakers who build their websites with AI assistants such as Claude or ChatGPT. Its guides are written so these assistants can read them directly, and Movity plans to launch an MCP server in the coming weeks. Once connected, an assistant will be able to build pages around a filmmaker’s work, embed videos, and pull posters and stills from the Movity library.

Current limitations

Some announced features are not available yet. Gear-based search is in development. An EU storage option, which lets European productions keep their footage on servers in the EU, is due in the coming weeks. The Movity mobile app is scheduled to launch in a few weeks, followed by an Apple TV app. The MCP server is also still to come. Movity plans regular in-person screenings in several major cities starting next year, but hasn’t named the cities yet.

A frame extractor – for free

Something else Movity is also offering is a free browser-based frame extractor that creates one full-resolution still from every detected shot in an MP4 or MOV file up to 15 minutes long. The tool compares frames to identify cuts, keeps a frame from the middle of each shot, and generates a color palette for every still as well as for the clip as a whole. The PNGs can be downloaded individually or as a ZIP. Because processing runs locally in the browser, the video isn’t uploaded and never leaves the user’s device. Nice!

Price and availability

Movity is available now at movity.io. The Free plan is free (as the name suggests) and therefore doesn’t require a credit card. It includes 2GB of storage, files up to 500MB, and HD streaming.

The Creator plan costs $12 per month billed annually ($144 per year) or $15 month-to-month and includes 250GB of storage, files up to 5GB, HD streaming, and analytics.

The Pro plan costs $24 per month billed annually ($288 per year) or $29 per month, with 500GB of storage, files up to 20GB, 4K streaming, per-viewer analytics, status workflows, and the option to remove Movity branding. Both paid plans come with a 7-day free trial. An Enterprise tier offers custom storage, SSO, and volume pricing is available for studios. Movity lists its prices in US dollars only.

For new users, you can get 15% off all plans (including yearly) until December 31, 2026, with the code: CINED15

Would you search for reference films by color and keyframe, and would a curated, human-made feed make you move your work away from Vimeo? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Viltrox Black Friday – Up to 20% Off AF 35mm F1.4 Pro, NexusFocus F1 and Monitors
entry.summary: Viltrox’s Black Friday sale is live! The Viltrox online store offers up to 20% off its lenses, flashes, monitors, and accessories, including the new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro and the NexusFocus F1, which adds autofocus to PL-mount cine lenses on Sony E-mount cameras. Plus, larger orders i
entry.content:
Viltrox’s Black Friday sale is live! The Viltrox online store offers up to 20% off its lenses, flashes, monitors, and accessories, including the new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro and the NexusFocus F1, which adds autofocus to PL-mount cine lenses on Sony E-mount cameras. Plus, larger orders include gifts, and any Viltrox monitor comes with an 8K HDMI cable for $5.

The sale runs from November 19 to November 30, 2026. The full 20% discount applies to the US store; customers in the EU, the UK, and Japan get up to 15% off under the regional terms. Let’s take a look at the highlights!

The new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro leads the lens deals

The AF 35mm F1.4 Pro for Sony E and Nikon Z launched on October 29. Viltrox applied its Black Friday price from launch, so the full-frame prime with VCM autofocus costs $663.20 (regular $829). The other full-frame Pro and LAB primes have the same discount: the AF 85mm F1.4 Pro is $478.40 (regular $598), and the AF 35mm F1.2 LAB is $799.20 (regular $999).

For APS-C cameras, the AF 56mm F1.2 Pro (85mm full-frame equivalent) is $464 (regular $580). Unless noted, prices in this article are for the Sony E versions in the US store. Other mounts are also on sale.

Smaller EVO and Air lenses

The two new APS-C telephoto primes in the EVO series use STM autofocus and have customizable controls. These links go to the Fujifilm X versions, and the Sony E versions cost the same:

  • AF 75mm F1.8 EVO: $263.20, down from $329
  • AF 90mm F2.2 EVO: $295.20, down from $369

The full-frame AF 26mm F2.8 EVO pancake lens, which we covered at its launch in July, weighs 130g / 4.6oz. The Black Friday prices are:

  • Black: $239.20, down from $299
  • Silver or gray with square hood: $255.20, down from $319

The APS-C AF 9mm F2.8 Air ultra-wide, with a 113.8° angle of view and a 0.13m / 5.1in minimum focus distance, is $159.20, down from $199.

NexusFocus F1: autofocus for PL lenses at 20% off

One of the most distinctive products in the Black Friday sale is the Viltrox NexusFocus F1 PL-E Autofocus Control System. Designed to bring modern autofocus capabilities to manual PL-mount cine lenses, including vintage glass, the system opens up new possibilities for filmmakers who want to combine the unique optical character of classic cine lenses with the convenience of autofocus.

By adapting PL-mount cine lenses, or lenses with a CineMod PL conversion, to Sony E-mount cameras, NexusFocus F1 uses external FIZ motors to control lens operation. Using the camera’s built-in PDAF and AI subject recognition, it enables Eye AF, face detection, subject tracking, and touch focus with traditionally manual cine lenses. This can be useful for solo filmmakers, independent cinematographers, documentary shooters, and small production crews working without a dedicated focus puller, as well as gimbal operators and event videographers who work in fast-paced shooting environments.

Unlike LiDAR-based autofocus solutions that rely on external ranging sensors, NexusFocus F1 uses the camera’s own autofocus data, which Viltrox says helps avoid potential parallax issues associated with external distance-measuring systems.

For now, NexusFocus F1 is designed exclusively for Sony E-mount cameras. The company recommends Sony camera bodies equipped with an AI processing unit for optimal subject recognition and autofocus performance. We tested the system earlier this year, so read our NexusFocus F1 review for a closer look at its real-world performance.

NexusFocus F1 uses external FIZ motors to operate different lens control rings, so users can configure the system to match their shooting needs. Depending on the number and placement of motors, the system can control:

  • Focus: Automates manual focusing, allowing the camera’s autofocus system to drive the lens for Eye AF, face detection, subject tracking, and touch focus.
  • Iris: Enables electronic aperture adjustment, giving users more convenient exposure control without manually turning the lens aperture ring.
  • Zoom: Supports motorized zoom operation for compatible zoom lenses, with smooth focal-length adjustments during shooting.

The available Single Motor and Dual Motor Packages determine how many functions can be controlled at the same time. A single motor can be assigned to one lens control ring, while the dual-motor setup lets you control two functions simultaneously, such as focus and iris or focus and zoom.

The NexusFocus app comes with a built-in lens database with preloaded calibration profiles for supported lenses. For lenses not included in the database, users can manually enter lens information and create their own calibration profiles through the app, which is currently available for iOS. The app also supports importing and managing multiple lens profiles, making it easier to switch between different lenses and shooting setups.

A backlit display on the adapter provides lens information, while side buttons give access to system menus. Sony’s Monitor & Ctrl app enables wireless monitoring and remote control from a compatible smartphone or tablet, including start/stop recording and adjustments to focus, iris, and zoom. Stills captured through the system retain EXIF data.

The adapter weighs 262g / 9.2oz, each motor 146.5g / 5.2oz, and the power box 62g / 2.2oz. The motors run on 6–18V via USB-C, while the power box supports 5–20V USB-C PD input. A D-Tap to USB-C cable is included. The adapter mount features dust sealing, and the detachable tripod foot includes a 1/4″ thread. Firmware updates can be installed wirelessly via Bluetooth through the app.

For Black Friday, the Single Motor Package is $479.20 (regular $599), and the Dual Motor Package is $719.20 (regular $899). Both packages include the PL-E adapter, power box, lens gears, mounting accessories, cables, and a carrying case.

Flashes, monitors, and free gifts

The Vintage Z1 Pro retro speedlite has a circular color touchscreen, TTL and manual modes, and High-Speed Sync up to 1/8000s. It costs $47.99 (regular $59.99) for Sony, Nikon, FUJIFILM, and Canon. The foldable Vintage Z2 mini flash weighs 52g / 1.8oz and is $28.79 (regular $35.99).

Viltrox monitors are also 20% off – for example, the DC-550 Pro II 5.5-inch monitor at $190.40 (regular $238). With any Viltrox monitor, customers can add the Viltrox 8K HDMI Cable for $5 (currently $10.39 on its own). You must add the cable to the cart manually.

Free gifts are also available on larger orders, calculated after discounts:

  • Orders of $350 or more: cleaning cloth set
  • Orders of $700 or more: lens pouch plus cleaning cloth set

If the cleaning cloth sets run out, Viltrox replaces them with an 8K HDMI cable. If the lens pouches run out, the replacement is a Vintage Z2 flash for the matching camera mount.

Price and availability

The Viltrox Black Friday sale ends on November 30, 2026. The prices above reflect the Viltrox US store as of November 23, 2026. In the EU, the UK, and Japan, discounts are up to 15%, so regional prices might differ. Gift availability depends on stock and Viltrox’s campaign terms.

Is the NexusFocus F1 at this price enough to bring your PL lenses to a Sony body, or is a new AF prime higher on your list? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Kodak Reports Growth in Motion Picture Film – The Odyssey Returns to IMAX 70mm in December
entry.summary: Kodak has reported a third quarter with higher revenue, higher profit, and less debt, and CEO Jim Continenza told investors that the company continues “to see growth in motion picture films.” Two days later, Universal confirmed that Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, shot completel
entry.content:
Kodak has reported a third quarter with higher revenue, higher profit, and less debt, and CEO Jim Continenza told investors that the company continues “to see growth in motion picture films.” Two days later, Universal confirmed that Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, shot completely on KODAK 65mm film, returns to theaters on December 11.

The two announcements are not connected, and Kodak’s CEO did not mention The Odyssey on the call. Together they still answer a question we asked fifteen months ago, when Kodak warned about its ability to continue as a going concern. The main supplier of motion picture camera film is in a much safer financial position, and the largest film-originated release of the year is still earning money for the format.

Kodak’s numbers for the third quarter

According to Kodak’s results release, revenue for the quarter was $276 million, up 3% from $269 million a year ago. Gross profit rose 7% to $73 million and GAAP net income was $21 million, compared with $13 million. The company held $317 million in cash at the end of September. Long-term debt is down to $108 million from $208 million at the end of 2025. After our report on the fourth straight quarter of growth in August, this is the fifth.

Film sits in the Advanced Materials and Chemicals segment, which grew 21% to $99 million and now makes up more than a third of Kodak’s revenue. The print business, still the largest segment, fell 7% to $165 million. In the release, Jim calls Advanced Materials and Chemicals “our fastest growing, most profitable unit.”

How much of the growth is motion picture film

The detail is in the quarterly filing, and it is more modest than the headline. Of the $17 million increase in segment revenue, Kodak attributes $8 million to higher volumes and $7 million to higher prices in Industrial Film and Chemicals. Higher volume in Motion Picture added $1 million. For the first nine months, Motion Picture added $2 million through volume and $2 million through price. Kodak does not publish a revenue figure for motion picture film alone.

So the statement on the call is correct, and the growth is small in dollars. According to the call transcripts, Jim said: “Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” and named Sense and Sensibility and Digger, the second of which was shot on KODAK film in VistaVision. His remark that Kodak now sells a range of films directly to distributors refers to still film, not to motion picture stock.

Two other points in the filing matter for productions. Kodak writes that demand for consumer film, equipment limits, and labor shortages led to backorders, and that new staff and equipment have reduced them. It also warns that more demand “may continue to place stress on manufacturing equipment and the labor force without further investment.” Total capital spending for 2026 is planned at $30 to $35 million. The filing has no going-concern language.

The Odyssey as a case for 65mm

Universal’s announcement puts the film back on “more than 1,000 screens in the U.S. and Canada in all formats, including IMAX and IMAX 70mm.” The studio gives the gross as $626 million in North America and $1.80 billion worldwide, which makes it the highest-grossing film for both Universal and Christopher Nolan. Universal does not say how many IMAX 70mm locations take part or how long the run lasts.

IMAX reported in its own third-quarter results that The Odyssey is its highest-grossing release, “with over $550 million in worldwide box office,” more than 30% of the film’s global total. Dune: Part Three opens on December 18 and is booked into IMAX theaters, so the IMAX window for the re-release is probably short.

For the film stock side, Kodak’s production report has the figures. The production “consumed over two million feet (379 miles) of 15-perf 65mm negative filmstock,” which is about 610km, all of it processed at FotoKem in Burbank. One IMAX 70mm print weighs about 600 lb (272kg) and is about 11 miles (17.7km) long. We described the cameras in our article on how Christopher Nolan shot The Odyssey on IMAX film.

Kodak’s current US price list shows $1,660 for a 1,000 ft (305m) roll of 65mm VISION3 500T. At that list price, two million feet of negative come to about $3.3 million, before processing and before any production discount. This is our calculation and not a figure from Kodak or Universal. It shows why one production of this size is visible in a business line that grows by one or two million dollars per quarter.

Supply is managed but not unlimited

Kodak changed how it sells 65mm stock this year. Since January, 1,000 ft rolls of VISION3 500T and 200T in 65mm are finished to order, with a minimum order of 16 rolls where it was one roll before. Kodak’s customer notice gives a delivery time of about three weeks in the US and Canada and about six weeks in Europe and Asia. Large productions can plan for that. A short or a music video that wants a few rolls of 65mm has a harder time.

The company continues to add products. It introduced KODAK VERITA 200D in the spring, and at this year’s Cannes festival it counted twenty productions shot on its film. For cinematographers, the practical result of this quarter is that the supplier is stable and the constraint has moved to factory capacity and lead times.

Have you shot on film this year, and did you have problems getting stock or lab time? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Soundsnap Joins MZed Black Friday 2026 – 3 Months Free, 550,000 Royalty-Free Sound Effects and Search by Tone
entry.summary: Our MZed Black Friday 2026 sale starts on Monday, and it comes with a partner I am really happy about: Soundsnap . Everyone who signs up for an annual MZed Pro membership during the sale gets three months of the royalty-free sound effects library for free, on top of the $199 sale
entry.content:
Our MZed Black Friday 2026 sale starts on Monday, and it comes with a partner I am really happy about: Soundsnap. Everyone who signs up for an annual MZed Pro membership during the sale gets three months of the royalty-free sound effects library for free, on top of the $199 sale price. Here is what Soundsnap is, why it is interesting for editors and sound designers, and how you get the offer.

For those of you who don’t know it yet, Soundsnap is a professional sound effects library built for post-production editors, sound designers and game audio professionals. According to the company, the catalog holds 550,000 sounds recorded in 126 countries, new content is added every week, and every sound is cleared for commercial and personal use. Soundsnap has been running for more than 15 years and calls itself “a library of libraries.” MZed is CineD’s education platform, and the three Soundsnap months come with the annual MZed Pro membership, which costs $199 instead of $349 during the sale. Full disclosure: Soundsnap is a partner of our MZed Black Friday sale.

From a TED talk to feature film soundtracks

Soundsnap was founded by Tasos Frantzolas, a sound designer whose TED talk “Everything you hear on film is a lie” is a good starting point if you want to understand how much of what we hear in films is created in post. Tasos contacted us through the MZed website in September, and it was clear quickly that the two platforms fit together: MZed has courses on editing and sound, and a sound effects library is the logical next tool after those lessons.

According to Soundsnap, the work of its sound designers runs through films including Black Swan, Star Trek, Mad Max: Fury Road, The Revenant, Dunkirk, Million Dollar Baby and Triangle of Sadness. A current example: one of the company’s sound designers traveled across Europe to record original sounds for The Odyssey.

Search by feeling, not only by keyword

The feature I find most interesting for editors is tone-based browsing. Next to the classic keyword search, Soundsnap lets you browse by emotional tone: Dark, Tense, Eerie, Ethereal, Bright, Subtle, Rhythmic, Futuristic, Building and Chaotic. If you have ever typed “whoosh” into a search field and scrolled through page after page of results, you know why this matters. When you cut a scene, you usually know how a moment should feel long before you know which literal sound you need, and a search that works the same way is much closer to how editors and sound designers think.

The library is also sorted into curated categories, among them cinematic transitions, user interface sounds, pulses and drones, trailer hits, ambiences and game sounds.

All annual Soundsnap plans also include AI Voiceover, with more than 10,000 voices that the company describes as realistic and an AI that, according to Soundsnap, understands emotion. For temp tracks, animatics and pitch videos, my feeling is that this can save a lot of back and forth before the real voice talent is booked.

The AI angle

There is another side to Soundsnap that says a lot about where our industry is heading. According to the company, top technology companies now license the Soundsnap catalog to train their AI audio models, and Soundsnap is one of the providers of audio for AI because of its large dataset and its rich metadata. Soundsnap does not name these companies (and yes, I would love to know which ones). My guess is that well-tagged and properly licensed audio will only become more valuable as AI audio tools grow, and a library that has collected and described its sounds for more than 15 years is in a strong position there.

For filmmakers, the licensing part is the more practical point: every sound in the library is cleared for commercial and personal use, so you can use it in client work without a separate license.

Who uses Soundsnap?

Soundsnap lists a long line of clients on its homepage. Among the agencies and creative studios are Wieden+Kennedy, Droga5, Ogilvy, R/GA, 72andSunny, Iris Worldwide, Rethink, BUCK, Stink Studios, Hello Monday and Zealot. Post houses and production companies include DNEG, Cut+Run, Cartel, Modern Post, Whitehouse Post, Florentine Films, Little Monster Films and Tremolo Productions. The list of larger companies and studios names Apple, Google, Netflix Animation, Disney, Pixar, Warner Bros., Nike, Spotify, Roku, The New York Times, Vox Media, Vice, BBC, ITV, Rockstar Games, Ubisoft, Supercell and Niantic.

How to get three months of Soundsnap for free

The offer is part of the MZed Black Friday 2026 sale, and getting it is simple:

  • Sign up for an annual MZed Pro membership during the sale, which starts on Monday, November 23, 2026. The sale price is $199 instead of $349.
  • After you join, you find the Soundsnap code in the MZed member area.
  • Redeem the code at soundsnap.com by February 1, 2027, and you get three months of Soundsnap for free.

The code is only available inside the MZed member area, so you will not find it on a public page. The Soundsnap months come on top of everything else MZed Pro includes: the full course library and member benefits such as B&H EDU Advantage pricing, which we announced earlier this month.

Do you already work with a sound effects library in your edits, or do you still record and build most of your sounds yourself? And would a search by tone change the way you look for sounds? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: FUJIFILM GFX ETERNA 55 Body-Only Version for $9,999 Now Up for Pre-order – Without Monitor, Top Handle, and AC Adapter
entry.summary: A second, cheaper way into FUJIFILM’s large-format cinema camera has appeared: the GFX ETERNA 55 is now listed as a body-only version for $9,999.95, which is $6,499 less than the standard package. The camera itself is the same 102MP, 4:3 open gate model. What you give up is the 5
entry.content:
A second, cheaper way into FUJIFILM’s large-format cinema camera has appeared: the GFX ETERNA 55 is now listed as a body-only version for $9,999.95, which is $6,499 less than the standard package. The camera itself is the same 102MP, 4:3 open gate model. What you give up is the 5-inch touchscreen monitor, the top handle, and the AC power adapter.

The body-only GFX ETERNA 55 appeared at retailers this week. B&H lists it as a new item for preorder, next to the standard version that stays on sale at $16,499. We have covered the camera closely since its launch, from the full specs and price announcement in September 2025 to Johnnie’s first-look review and mini-documentary, its IMAX certification, and the firmware 1.10 roadmap.

What is in the box, and what is not

According to the B&H listing, the body-only version ships with the camera body (FUJIFILM G mount), one NP-W235 battery (7.2V, 2200mAh), a body cap, the ARRI PL mount adapter, and a two-year limited warranty. The PL adapter stays in the box, so owners of PL glass do not lose anything on the lens side.

The standard $16,499 package adds the 5-inch touchscreen LCD monitor, its hood and mount, the top handle, and the AC-15VS AC power adapter with AC cable. In other words, the $6,500 difference covers the monitor and the parts that hold and power it on a basic build.

Who is this version for?

Many productions rig the GFX ETERNA 55 in a cage with their own handles, power, and monitoring. ARRI has a dedicated cage system for the camera, and image and RAW output go to external monitors and recorders over SDI and HDMI. For rental houses and owner-operators with that equipment, the standard package carried parts they did not use.

FUJIFILM’s own VF-GFXC2 viewfinder connects through the same ETERNA Multi-Pin connector as the included monitor, and it attaches with the same monitor mount. At IBC, FUJIFILM told us that bundles with the EVF, the monitor, or both were under discussion. The body-only version is now one answer to that. Buyers who plan to use the VF-GFXC2 should check which mounting parts come with the viewfinder, because the body-only package does not include the monitor mount.

Same camera

Nothing changes on the camera side. The GFX ETERNA 55 uses the 102MP GFX CMOS II HS sensor (43.8 x 32.9mm, 55mm diagonal) with dual base ISO 800 and 3200, a built-in electronic variable ND from ND0.6 to ND2.1, and recording up to DCI 8K at 30fps or 4K 4:3 open gate at 48fps. Internal codecs include Apple ProRes 422 HQ and 10-bit 4:2:2 H.265, and the camera outputs 12-bit RAW to external recorders.

Price and availability

The FUJIFILM GFX ETERNA 55 body-only version is available for preorder at $9,999.95 at B&H. CVP lists the body for preorder at € 9,149 (excluding VAT) at CVP. The standard version with monitor, top handle, and AC adapter stays at $16,499 at B&H. A shipping date is not listed yet. For more information, see the FUJIFILM website.

Does $9,999 make the GFX ETERNA 55 more interesting for you, or would you have kept the monitor and handle? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.content:
HONOR starts the global rollout of the Magic9 Pro Max in Malaysia, with more markets to follow in the coming weeks. The phone records ARRI LogC3 in ARRI Wide Gamut 3 with 10-bit color in a dedicated ARRI CINEMA Mode, uses two 200MP rear cameras, and records APV 10-bit 4:2:2, while new teleconverters, a SmallRig video kit and gimbals go on sale alongside it.

We have previously reported on the technical collaboration between ARRI and HONOR, on the HONOR Robot Phone as its first product, and on the launch of the Magic9 Pro Max in China in September. I also filmed with the phone in Los Angeles for our HONOR Magic9 Pro Max first look, which covers the ARRI CINEMA Mode interface and my list of current shortcomings in detail. With the Malaysian launch, HONOR now releases the global spec sheet, the first international price, and the accessory lineup for markets outside China. The Magic9 Pro Max also marks the tenth anniversary of the HONOR Magic Series.

HONOR describes the phone’s imaging pipeline as an “end-to-end professional cinema workflow co-engineered with ARRI.” In practice, ARRI’s contribution is color management: sensor calibration, the LogC3 encoding, and the ARRI Looks. The optics, the sensors, and the processing come from HONOR.

What ARRI CINEMA Mode records

In ARRI CINEMA Mode, the Magic9 Pro Max records up to 4K at 60fps with the ARRI LogC3 curve, 10-bit color depth, and ARRI Wide Gamut 3. This is the encoding of the ALEXA Mini and AMIRA generation, so existing LogC3 conversion LUTs and color-managed timelines in grading applications work with the footage. The mode puts exposure, focus, frame rate, codec, and monitoring controls into one interface.

For recording, HONOR uses the APV codec at 10-bit 4:2:2. According to HONOR, APV files use about 20% less storage than ProRes at a similar image-quality target, depending on the recording settings and test conditions. APV support also comes from the Snapdragon platform, and editing applications such as LumaFusion for Android and DaVinci Resolve already decode it. (Adobe Premiere, not!)

The phone has 14 preset ARRI Looks: two ARRI conversion Looks and 12 stylized Looks. All of them are available as a real-time preview while you record in LogC3, or they can be burned into the recording. The ARRI Look Library adds 87 predefined creative grades, and the phone also accepts third-party LogC3 LUTs.

Dual 200MP cameras and the HONOR Imaging Chip H1

The main camera uses a 200MP 1/1.28-inch sensor behind an f/1.57 lens with OIS and what HONOR calls 3-degree gimbal-level stabilization. The telephoto camera also has 200MP, with a 1/1.4-inch sensor, an f/2.6 lens, and OIS. HONOR rates both cameras at CIPA 8.0 for stabilization. A 50MP ultra-wide camera with an f/2.0 lens completes the rear module. In our first look, the ultra-wide camera was not available in ARRI CINEMA Mode.

Image processing runs on the self-developed HONOR Imaging Chip H1, which is made on a 6nm process and rated at 18.8 TOPS/W. According to HONOR, the chip applies AI noise reduction in the RAW domain in real time. HONOR’s test data claims an 8dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio and up to 14 stops of dynamic range. These are manufacturer figures, and we have not measured the phone in our lab yet.

Outside ARRI CINEMA Mode, the phone records 4K at up to 120fps in supported modes. On the front, a 55MP f/2.0 camera uses a square sensor format. You can hold the phone upright and still reframe the shot for vertical or horizontal deliverables later.

Cinematic LiveVideo and Magic Color

Cinematic LiveVideo is a short-clip function inside ARRI CINEMA Mode. A press and hold on the shutter captures three seconds of motion at up to 4K, in 16:9 or 2.39:1, with the active ARRI Look applied and an optional ARRI watermark. Magic Color for Video takes a different approach to color: it analyzes the color of a reference clip and applies a matching look to new footage, which helps to keep shots consistent across a sequence.

Four microphones for directional sound

For audio, HONOR combines one directional microphone with three omnidirectional microphones. According to HONOR, this Cinematic Directional Microphone isolates a chosen sound source at distances of up to 20m / 66ft and suppresses sound outside a ±60° range. Four directional presets and a custom mode are available for interviews, performances, and location sound. Mind you that audio levels cannot be controlled manually in any of the video recording modes.

Teleconverters, a SmallRig kit and two gimbals

HONOR announces a set of optional creation tools for the international launch, and they go on sale together with the phone. The HONOR Teleconverter G200 is a 200mm add-on lens that measures about 81mm / 3.2in in length and weighs about 88g / 3.1oz. HONOR calls it the smallest and lightest 200mm smartphone teleconverter. The HONOR Teleconverter G500 has a 500mm equivalent focal length, which HONOR says is the longest of any smartphone teleconverter. HONOR names stage performances and wildlife as typical subjects for it.

The HONOR SmallRig Mobile Video Kit is a cage with mounting points for additional filming accessories, and it includes a cooling accessory for longer recordings. A handheld smart gimbal and an external mini-gimbal complete the accessory range.

Design, display and performance

The design takes its cue from the three-lens turret of the ARRIFLEX cameras, which date back to 1937. The 1+2 camera arrangement combines one large camera ring with two smaller lenses to group the main, telephoto, and ultra-wide cameras. The all-metal unibody measures 161.64 x 76.98 x 8.59mm / 6.36 x 3.03 x 0.34in and weighs 233g / 8.2oz. The phone is rated IP68, IP69, and IP69K for water and dust resistance.

The 6.8-inch LTPO OLED display has a resolution of 1320 x 2868 pixels, a refresh rate of 1 to 120Hz, 100% DCI-P3 coverage, and 4,320Hz PWM dimming. HONOR specifies up to 10,000 nits peak brightness, 2,000 nits full-screen brightness and a reflectance of 1.5%, with an anti-reflective coating and the HONOR Anti-Scratch NanoCrystal Shield. For a phone that is also its own monitor, the low reflectance is the more relevant figure for outdoor work.

The phone runs on the 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 with a Qualcomm Oryon CPU at up to 5GHz. The global spec sheet lists an 8,000mAh silicon-carbon battery (typical value, rated at 7,745mAh) with 100W wired and 80W wireless HONOR SuperCharge. MagicOS 11 is based on Android 17. A dedicated AI Button opens HONOR’s AI agents, Google Lens and Gemini, and HONOR Connect adds file sharing with Insta360 devices and support for the AirDrop framework.

Current limitations

ARRI CINEMA Mode records at up to 4K 60fps, while 4K 120fps is limited to other recording modes. The dynamic range and noise figures come from HONOR’s own tests. In our first look, the ultra-wide camera was not available in ARRI CINEMA Mode, recorded audio levels could not be set manually, and stabilization could not be switched off completely. Battery capacity depends on the region: the global spec sheet lists 8,000mAh, while the Chinese model has 8,800mAh.

Price and availability

In Malaysia, the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max costs RM5,999 (about $1,460 / €1,330 at current exchange rates) with 24GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. HONOR counts 12GB of HONOR Turbo RAM in the 24GB figure, so this is the 12GB+512GB configuration of the global spec sheet. Colors are Shadow Black, Glacier Silver, and Moss Green. In selected regions, Pre-orders run from November 24 to December 3, 2026. Other markets will follow in the coming weeks, but HONOR has not announced its prices yet. The Magic9 Pro Max will not be available in the US. In Europe, distribution moves to 2027, and HONOR has not given an exact date yet. For more information, please visit the HONOR Malaysia website.

Would LogC3, ARRI Looks and APV recording on a phone change how you shoot B-roll or behind-the-scenes footage? Or does a dedicated camera still make more sense? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.summary: Nikon has released firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, the first major update for its full-frame cinema camera. The free download brings RED’s Log3G10 to H.265 recording, selectable High ISO noise reduction, 3D LUT output over HDMI, and more assignable controls. Caution! Do n
entry.content:
Nikon has released firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, the first major update for its full-frame cinema camera. The free download brings RED’s Log3G10 to H.265 recording, selectable High ISO noise reduction, 3D LUT output over HDMI, and more assignable controls.

Caution! Do not update the camera firmware with lenses other than Z-mount NIKKOR lenses or mount adapters other than FTZ II/FTZ attached; failure to observe this precaution could result in camera malfunction.

We covered the full feature list when Nikon detailed firmware 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, and the limitations that Nikon later listed on its firmware page in a follow-up article. Here is a summary of what owners get now that the firmware is out.

H.265 gets the R3D NE color pipeline

With firmware 2.00 (download link here), the ZR can record H.265 in Log3G10 gamma and the REDWideGamutRGB color gamut. These are the same gamma and gamut that the camera uses for R3D NE RAW, so H.265 clips can go through the same LUTs and grading setup as RAW footage from the ZR or from RED cameras. Until now, the only log option in H.265 was Nikon’s N-Log.

The High ISO NR setting now has four levels: Off, Low, Normal, and High. It is available in H.265 with Log3G10, H.265 with N-Log, and ProRes 422 HQ with N-Log. In our Nikon ZR Lab Test, the internal noise reduction in H.265 N-Log was very strong, so the option to lower it or switch it off is a practical change for anyone who prefers to denoise in post. Nikon also says that firmware 2.00 suppresses black-level fluctuation between frames, which reduces flicker in dark areas of the image.

Monitoring and controls

Focus peaking now stays visible when the ZR records R3D NE with a LUT applied. The camera can also send a 3D LUT over HDMI to an external monitor. According to Nikon, this has three conditions: the HDMI output drops to Full HD when a LUT is applied, the image refresh rate is halved at 60p and 50p (the output frame rate stays at 60p or 50p), and the HDMI signal can disconnect with some video settings. The rear monitor is not affected by these limits.

An Fn button can now switch the monitor between the selected LUT and the flat log image via View Assist. During recording, View Assist can be switched, but the 3D LUT itself cannot be turned on or off. The command dials can now be assigned to ISO, exposure compensation, white balance, and color temperature.

Open gate and anamorphic de-squeeze planned for 2027

Two of the most requested features are not part of this firmware. When Nikon announced the development of firmware 2.00, it also said that it is developing open gate recording and a de-squeeze display for anamorphic lenses, intending to add them to the ZR in 2027. Nikon has not given a version number or a date for that firmware yet. For more on how the camera performs on set, see our Nikon ZR review.

Price and availability

Firmware 2.00 for the Nikon ZR is a free download from the Nikon Download Center. The Nikon ZR body is available for 2,196.95 at B&H, and for €1,988.10 ex VAT or €2,405.60 inc VAT at CVP. For more information, please visit the Nikon website.

Our once-a-year sale on MZed starts today: an annual MZed Pro membership costs $199 instead of $349, for a limited time, and it renews at $199 per year. This year, the membership also comes with a Black Friday goodie bag from our partners, with 40% off ShotDeck, three months of Soundsnap for free, 60% off Filmstro, B&H education pricing and two free e-books. Here is what is in it, and what is coming to MZed next.

MZed, our filmmaking education platform, has launched its annual Black Friday sale. MZed offers expert filmmaking courses, taught by filmmakers. The courses come from working DPs, editors, directors and colorists, together with the ARRI Academy and AbelCine.

What the $199 includes

One MZed Pro membership opens almost every course and lesson on the platform. Right now that is 71 courses with 937 lessons and 385 hours of video from 36 educators and teaching teams. New courses that we release during your membership year are included from the day they go live, at no extra cost. You can stream on the web or download lessons to the MZed iOS app to watch offline, and most courses come with a certificate of completion.

Among the educators are many ASC level cinematographers, Philip Bloom, Oscar-winning editor Tom Cross, ACE, Alex Buono, Ollie Kenchington, Tal Lazar, Mascha Deikova, Seth Worley, Adam Epstein, Doug Jensen, Drew Geraci, Kitty Peters, Digby Hogan, Vincent Laforet and Rubidium Wu, plus the ARRI Academy and AbelCine. The library is sorted into four subject areas: Cinematography Mastery (cameras, lenses, lighting), Visual Storytelling & Directing (story, framing, directing), Post-Production & Color (editing, grading, sound) and AI Workflows (AI video, masking, subtitles).

New this year: the Black Friday goodie bag

This is the part that changed compared to earlier years. Everyone who buys a new annual membership or renews an annual membership during the sale gets these partner benefits:

  • ShotDeck: 40% off an annual plan. ShotDeck is the library of film stills that directors and cinematographers use to find and share visual references, and it relaunched recently with natural language search and movie and TV clips.
  • Soundsnap: three months for free. The library holds 550,000 royalty-free sound effects, all cleared for commercial use.
  • Filmstro: 60% off any Filmstro annual plan. Filmstro makes adaptive music that you can shape to your edit, and it also works inside Premiere Pro.
  • B&H EDU Advantage: education pricing at B&H on cameras, lenses, lighting and more. We announced this benefit earlier this month. To use it, opt in under Member Discounts in your MZed account by December 7, 2026. It is available only where B&H ships.
  • Free downloads from MZed educators, among them the Timelapse Field Guide by Drew Geraci and The CineD Lab Test Compendium 2026 Edition, the e-book with our camera lab tests, which normally costs $29.

You find the codes, the downloads and the sign-up steps in the MZed member area after you join. We do not publish the codes anywhere else, so please do not look for them on a public page.

Honestly, if you use two of these benefits, the membership has almost paid for itself.

What is coming next on MZed?

New courses are part of your membership from the day of release, and there are several in the pipeline. Mastering Visual Podcasts with Ollie Kenchington shows how to light, shoot and cut a podcast that people want to watch, from a single host to a full round table.

High-Speed Filmmaking is a course that Ariel Levesque and I are working on about super slow motion, from the plan for a shot to the delivery, filmed on real shoots with the real numbers. It has five lessons, the first one arrives within the next weeks, and it is supported by Pixboom. This one is free for everyone with an MZed account, so you do not even need MZed Pro for it.

We are also working on editing a masterclass with Cory Geryak from the ARRI Academy at Camerimage. Its working title is Lighting the Scene.

For the business side, Know Your Rate is about pricing your work as a filmmaker, and it’s coming in 2027.

Black Friday is the only sale we run on MZed all year, so if you have thought about joining, this is the moment.

entry.content:
SIRUI has introduced the PC03 ScopeGrip, a 3x telephoto lens kit for the iPhone 16 Pro, 17 Pro and 18 Pro models. The kit combines an optical telephoto attachment with a camera-style photography grip and a wireless Bluetooth remote, and SIRUI designed the system for compact, all-in-one storage.

Most of our SIRUI coverage focuses on camera lenses, most recently the Aurora 15mm F1.6 and 24mm F1.4 autofocus primes. However, the company also makes mobile accessories, such as the VD-01 1.33x anamorphic lens for smartphones. Add-on telephoto lenses for the iPhone are not new either. We have previously reported on the SANDMARC Telephoto Tetraprism lens and on Tilta’s T-mount iPhone lenses. With the ScopeGrip, SIRUI sells the lens, a grip, and a remote as a single kit.

3x optical magnification

According to SIRUI, the core of the kit is a 3x optical telephoto lens that extends the reach of compatible iPhone cameras. Unlike digital zoom, the extra magnification comes from a physical lens system, so the image is enlarged before it reaches the phone’s sensor. SIRUI names distant subjects, outdoor scenes and travel photography as typical uses.

In SIRUI’s product photos, the lens attaches to a dedicated iPhone case, and the grip connects to the back of that case. The press release does not say which of the iPhone’s rear cameras the lens is made for. It also gives no resulting focal length, no information on the optical design, and no weight.

Camera-style grip and Bluetooth remote

The second part of the kit is a dedicated photography grip. SIRUI says its camera-inspired design gives a more secure and comfortable hold. This matters most at longer focal lengths, where small hand movements are more visible in the frame.

The product photos show a shutter button and a USB-C port on top of the grip, and a threaded socket on its base. The kit also includes a wireless Bluetooth remote that triggers the iPhone camera without a touch on the screen. SIRUI lists tripod work, group photos and self-portraits as applications, and any situation where camera movement must stay to a minimum. The press text is about stills photography. It does not say whether the remote also starts and stops video recording.

Specifications

Lens:

According to SIRUI’s spec sheet, the 3x Telephoto Lens has 12 elements in 9 groups. The field of view is 157m at a distance of 1,000m / 515ft at 3,281ft. The lens measures 61 x 34 x 34mm / 2.40 x 1.34 x 1.34in, weighs 73.8g / 0.16lb, and has an IPX4 water resistance rating. To mount it, users align the red dots and turn the lens 90° clockwise until it locks.

The grip with the Bluetooth remote:

Is made of ABS + PC, aluminum alloy and silicone. For the iPhone 16 Pro, 17 Pro and 18 Pro, it weighs 117.2g / 0.26lb and measures 130.3 x 48.1 x 88.8mm / 5.13 x 1.89 x 3.50in. The Pro Max version weighs 120.2g / 0.27lb and measures 139.3 x 48.1 x 88.8mm / 5.48 x 1.89 x 3.50in. The remote has a 30mAh battery at 3.7V, charges via USB-C, and runs for up to 20 hours, with a wireless range of 10m / 33ft and an operating temperature of -10 to 45°C / 14 to 113°F.

The phone case:

Uses the same materials as the grip. It weighs 60.2g / 0.13lb and measures 155.1 x 22 x 78.2mm / 6.11 x 0.87 x 3.08in for the Pro models, and 68.9g / 0.15lb and 168.4 x 22 x 84.1mm / 6.63 x 0.87 x 3.31in for the Pro Max models.

Price and availability

The PC03 ScopeGrip Series 3x Telephoto Lens Kit is compatible with the iPhone 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max, the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, and the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Pricing, regional availability, and purchasing information will be announced through SIRUI’s official sales channels.

entry.summary: KONDOR BLUE has teamed up with filmmaker and YouTuber Mark Fischbach, better known as Markiplier, on a modular rigging system for GoPro’s MISSION 1 cameras. It consists of a cage with a swing-away access door and dual NATO rails, a Media I/O Hub with full-size HDMI and three USB-
entry.content:
KONDOR BLUE has teamed up with filmmaker and YouTuber Mark Fischbach, better known as Markiplier, on a modular rigging system for GoPro’s MISSION 1 cameras. It consists of a cage with a swing-away access door and dual NATO rails, a Media I/O Hub with full-size HDMI and three USB-C ports for audio, timecode and power, and the Power Grip 550 that runs on NP-F550 batteries. Fischbach did not just lend his name; he has invested his own money in the project.

The KONDOR BLUE × Markiplier system is designed for all three cameras of the MISSION 1 series: the MISSION 1, the MISSION 1 PRO and the interchangeable-lens MISSION 1 PRO ILS. The idea is simple and, in my opinion, the right one for these cameras: you start with a compact cage for handheld work and add mounting, media and power only when the shoot calls for it. The three parts are sold separately at $100 for the cage, $95 for the Media I/O Hub and $80 for the Power Grip 550.

A YouTuber, a cage maker and a camera company in transition

The background story is hard to separate from the product. We reported in September that Fischbach had become GoPro’s largest single shareholder with an 8.5% stake, at a time when GoPro was in its sale process. That process ended with the $285 million sale to Starman Optical, a buyer that does not make cameras, and Nick Woodman has since written that the cameras are staying. According to KONDOR BLUE, Fischbach’s investment in GoPro became public only after the collaboration on this rig had already started.

That collaboration began on the Universal Studios backlot in June 2026, where Fischbach met KONDOR BLUE founder Lukas Colombo. Fischbach was already a KONDOR BLUE customer. In the short video in the press kit, he says that he knew he wanted to use the ILS version of the GoPro and wanted accessories for it. His description of the process: “When I talked to you guys, it was actually design first. What is the problem that needs to be solved? It was an engineering-first mindset.”

Colombo, who founded the company as a working director and cinematographer, puts it like this: “When Mark and I started talking, I recognized that instinct immediately. He had a clear idea of how he wanted to use the new ILS cameras, so together we built the system around it.” On why he put money into the project, Fischbach says: “If I go into something and other people are willing to put the manpower behind designing, and all these kinds of things, the least I could do is try to make sure, on a financial level, I’m backing it as well.”

The MISSION 1 cage

The cage is the base of the system. Its swing-away access door lets you change batteries and microSD cards without taking the camera out of the cage, which is the one feature I would check first on any action camera cage. There are integrated NATO rails on the top and on the left side for handles, monitors and other accessories, and the side rib of the cage has an integrated carry loop, so you can grab the rig without adding a handle.

The renders also show a bubble level on the top plate, M4 threads on the front, a marking for the optical center on the bottom and Fischbach’s signature engraved on the back. KONDOR BLUE lists compatibility with the MISSION 1, MISSION 1 PRO and MISSION 1 PRO ILS, so one cage covers the whole lineup.

Media I/O Hub: full-size HDMI, audio, timecode and power

For me, the Media I/O Hub is the most interesting part of the system. It attaches under the cage and gives you a full-size HDMI video output plus three USB-C ports, labeled Audio In, TC In and Power In. Full-size HDMI is a big deal on set, because micro and mini HDMI connectors are the first thing to fail when a monitor cable gets pulled. KONDOR BLUE says that the hub is also compatible with smartphones and other devices with full-size HDMI or USB-C.

What KONDOR BLUE has not published yet is how the hub talks to the camera, which signals the camera accepts on each port, and whether there are any limits on simultaneous use. My guess is that it routes the camera’s own connections to sturdier ports rather than adding new functions, but that is just my guess. I hope KONDOR BLUE posts a detailed connection diagram on the product page at launch (dear KONDOR BLUE, a short video that shows timecode sync with a common TC box would answer most questions in two minutes).

Power Grip 550

The Power Grip 550 is a full-hand side grip that holds an NP-F550 battery to keep the camera running longer. It also has a USB-C power output, so it can feed the camera or another device on the rig. The renders show a battery level indicator on the side and a mounting point on top of the grip.

NP-F batteries are cheap, easy to find, and many of us already have a drawer full of them for monitors and lights, so this choice makes a lot of sense. Capacity and runtime figures with the MISSION 1 cameras are not part of the press material yet.

Who is it for?

GoPro calls the MISSION 1 family compact cinema cameras. When the series was announced at NAB 2026, it came with a 1-inch 50MP sensor, 8K60 recording and, on the PRO ILS, a Micro Four Thirds mount. We gave the MISSION 1 PRO ILS one of our CineD Best-of-Show Awards at NAB 2026, and GoPro later added anamorphic lens support through GoPro Labs. Once you put a real lens on the ILS, the camera needs proper support, power and a monitor output, and that is the gap this system fills.

KONDOR BLUE is not the first cage maker to take these cameras seriously. XLCS Designs showed its one-piece STORMWARDEN cage for the MISSION 1 PRO ILS at IBC 2026. The KONDOR BLUE approach is more modular, with dedicated I/O and power parts, and it follows the same thinking as the company’s Nikon ZR cage. The company has had a busy year in general: it acquired Element Filters and launched an optics division.

One note: the product photos also show a top handle with cold shoe and 1/4″-20 threads. It is not one of the three products on the launch price list, so check the product page for what is included before you order.

Price and availability

KONDOR BLUE lists the GoPro MISSION 1 Cage at $100, the Media I/O Hub at $95 and the Power Grip 550 at $80. The camera, batteries and the body cap seen in the images are sold separately. The products are announced today, November 19, 2026, and the full details, including supported models, pricing and availability, are on the KONDOR BLUE product page. At the time of writing, B&H and CVP did not list the system yet.

Do you use a GoPro MISSION 1 camera on your productions, and would you rig it up like this? Is a full-size HDMI and timecode hub the missing piece for you, or do you prefer to keep the camera as small as possible? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

  • Two PavoSlim 60B panels with a Forza 60B II: $1,063.20, down from $1,329

The PavoSlim 120C gets the largest discount at 25%, bringing the price from $799 down to $599.25. The 2 x 1 RGBWW panel is 1.85cm / 0.73in thick and gives up to 12,830 lux at 1m / 3.3ft. It has CCT, HSI, RGBW, Gel and Effect modes, and supports CRMX, Bluetooth and 2.4G wireless control. The included pop-up softbox comes with 1.5-stop and 2.5-stop diffusers and an eggcrate.

FS-60B and FS-300B bi-color monolights

The FS-60B is 20% off, which brings it from $109 to $87.20. The compact 70W monolight covers 2,700K to 6,500K and gives up to 13,360 lux at 1m / 3.3ft with the included 45° reflector. The power supply is built in, so one AC cable runs the light. It uses NANLITE’s FM mount, and a Bowens adapter is in the box. Control is onboard, through the NANLINK app via Bluetooth, or via 2.4G.

The FS-300B is $70 off, at $179 instead of $249. It is a 300W bi-color COB light with the same 2,700K–6,500K range and a Bowens mount. NANLITE rates it at 38,720 lux at 1m / 3.3ft with the included 45° reflector, and at CRI 96 and TLCI 97. The light has a metal yoke, a built-in umbrella holder, Bluetooth, and 2.4G control. When we covered the FS-300B launch, we saw it as an alternative to the Forza 300B.

FC-720C full-color spotlight

The largest saving in dollar terms applies to the FC-720C, which is $210 off at $539 instead of $749. The 750W Bowens mount spotlight uses NANLITE’s Nebula C4 light engine with a CCT range of 2,400K to 12,000K and ±150 green/magenta adjustment. With the included 45° reflector, NANLITE rates it at 11,400 lux at 3m / 9.8ft. It has five lighting modes, 460 LEE and ROSCO gel presets, 15 effects, and dimming in 0.1% steps. Control is onboard, through the NANLINK app or via DMX/RDM, and a carrying case is included.

PavoTube II 6CP

The next deal applies to the PavoTube II 6CP: $10 off, for $79 instead of $89. The 25cm / 10in tube also uses the Nebula C4 engine (2,400K–12,000K, ±150 G/M) and gives 661 lux at 0.5m / 1.6ft at 5600K. Compared with the PavoTube II 6C, it has a larger 3200mAh battery, NFC pairing with the NANLINK app, and stronger built-in magnets. It has 1/4″-20 threads on both ends, works with T12 clips, and includes 460 gel presets, 15 effects, and 8 group effects.

Price and availability

The NANLITE Black Friday deals start on November 20 and will run until December 3 on the NANLITE US online store.

Are you planning to add a PavoSlim panel or an FC-720C to your kit this Black Friday? Which NANLITE light would you pick from this list? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: DZOFILM Black Friday 2026 – 7th Anniversary Sale with Up to 38% Off, Arcana Kit Deal and New Education Kits
entry.summary: DZOFILM celebrates its 7th anniversary with its largest Black Friday sale so far. The promotion runs until December 3, 2026, with discounts of up to 38.89% on single lenses and sets, and savings of up to $4,660 on select kits. A limited Arcana 3-lens kit offer, three new bundles
entry.content:
DZOFILM celebrates its 7th anniversary with its largest Black Friday sale so far. The promotion runs until December 3, 2026, with discounts of up to 38.89% on single lenses and sets, and savings of up to $4,660 on select kits. A limited Arcana 3-lens kit offer, three new bundles for students and new owners, and two Instagram campaigns are also part of the event.

DZOFILM was founded in 2019, and its original Vespid primes arrived in October 2020. Since then, the lineup has grown into compact primes, anamorphics, zooms, macro lenses, and probe lenses. This year’s Black Friday early access phase started on October 20, and the deals run on the DZOFILM Black Friday page, in the DZOFILM official store, and through global DZOFILM dealers.

According to DZOFILM, the sale covers the full range, from the Vespid series to the two newest product lines: the Arcana 1.5x anamorphic primes and the Arles Zoom. The press release gives these maximum savings per category:

  • Primes (Arles and Vespid series): save up to $2,889
  • Anamorphic (Pavo series): up to 38.89% off
  • Macro (X-tract probe and Gnosis series): up to 37.15% off
  • Zooms: up to 22.49% off
  • Accessories: $100 off most Octopus adapters

Arcana 3-lens kit offer

The main offer of the campaign is the Arcana 3-lens kit with the 32mm, 45mm, and 75mm T2.1. Until December 1, 2026, the kit costs $2,699, which is $200 less than the regular price of $2,899. DZOFILM says the offer is for a limited time and a limited quantity. Single Arcana lenses stay at $1,099 each.

We covered the Arcana introduction in March 2026 and had a hands-on with the trio at NAB 2026. The lenses use a front anamorphic design with a 1.5x squeeze, and a 14-blade elliptical iris gives out-of-focus highlights that DZOFILM compares to a 2x anamorphic. They cover full frame with a 43.3mm image circle, and the flare coating is the neutral coating from the Pavo series, so the streaks take the color of the light source.

All three lenses have an 80mm front diameter, a 77mm filter thread, a length of 80mm, and a weight of approximately 700g / 1.54lb, with a difference of only 14g between them. This makes focal length changes on a gimbal or a DJI Ronin 4D possible without a new balance. The lenses ship in ARRI PL mount, with 0.8 MOD gears and a 270° focus throw.

A year with two Best-of-Show awards

DZOFILM connects the anniversary with a year of awards. The Arcana series received a CineD Best-of-Show Award at NAB 2026, and the Arles Zoom pair received a CineD Best-of-Show Award at IBC 2026. For the Arles Zoom, two points decided the award: the intentional overlap of the two zooms between 65mm and 75mm, and color science that matches the Arles primes.

Arles primes and the Arles Zoom

The Arles primes launched in June 2024 with five T1.4 lenses, and the 18mm T1.4 completed the series with 11 focal lengths in November 2025. The primes cover a 46.5mm VistaVision image circle and have a clean, corrected rendering. Most are T1.4, with the exception of the 14mm (T1.9), the 135mm (T1.8), and the 180mm (T2.4). In DZOFILM’s Instagram vote for the community’s favorite series, the Arles primes came first.

These are the Arles prime deals in the DZOFILM store:

  • Arles 25mm, 35mm, 40mm, 50mm, 75mm, and 100mm T1.4: $1,799 each (regular price $1,999)
  • Arles 14mm T1.9 and 18mm T1.4: $2,199 each (regular price $2,399)
  • Arles 21mm T1.4 and 135mm T1.8: $2,099 each (regular price $2,299)
  • Arles 180mm T2.4: $1,899 (regular price $2,399)
  • Arles 5-lens set (25/35/50/75/100mm): $7,499 (regular price $8,899)
  • Arles 5-lens B set (14/21/40/135/180mm): $8,499 (regular price $9,999)
  • Arles 10-lens set: $15,999 (regular price $18,888)

The Arles Zoom 25-75mm and 65-180mm T2.6 arrived in September 2026. Both are parfocal, keep T2.6 through the full zoom range, and weigh less than 1.8kg / 4lb. They share the 95mm front diameter, the M86 filter thread, and the gear positions of the primes. Unlike the primes, they cover a 43.5mm full-frame image circle, not VistaVision. The single zooms are not discounted and stay at $2,899 each, or $5,199 for the pair.

The Arles Zoom is part of the new Arles kit, which DZOFILM’s sale page lists as the Arles Series Creator Kit. It combines the 25-75mm zoom with the 18mm or the 14mm prime for $4,079 (listed as $4,769). A Pro version with the 25-75mm, the 18mm, and the 100mm costs $5,799.

Vespid Prime 2 and the education kits

The Vespid Prime 2 has six focal lengths from 18mm to 105mm, all at T1.9. Compared to the first generation, the lenses are approximately 20% lighter, and they send Cooke /i metadata through a built-in LEMO connector. They ship in PL mount only. We used the Vespid 2 lenses in our Nikon ZR review and mini-documentary.

  • Vespid Prime 2 24mm, 35mm, 50mm, 85mm, and 105mm: $999 each (regular price $1,199)
  • Vespid Prime 2 18mm: $1,099 (regular price $1,299)
  • Vespid Prime 2 6-lens set: $5,499 (regular price $6,289)
  • Original Vespid Prime T2.1: from $699 per lens (regular price $799), 9-lens set $5,899 (regular price $6,999)

The press release names three new bundles for this sale: the Arles Educational Kit, the Catta Educational Kit, and the Vespid 2 Three-Lens Kit. In addition to the Arles kit above, DZOFILM’s sale page lists these bundles:

  • Education kit with the Catta Ace 35-80mm zoom and the Vespid Prime 2 18mm and 24mm: $2,999 (listed as $3,869)
  • Vespid Prime 2 3-lens Versatile Kit (18/35/50mm): $2,799 (listed as $3,329)
  • Vespid Prime 2 3-lens Essential Kit (35/50/85mm): $2,699 (listed as $3,239)

The Catta Ace education kit is the source of the 22.49% maximum discount in the zoom category.

Pavo anamorphic discounts

The highest percentage discount is on the Pavo 2x anamorphic series for Super 35. DZOFILM released the first six Pavo lenses in 2023 (28mm to 100mm) at $5,499 per lens, and added a Macro 65mm, a 135mm, and a 180mm in 2024. The lenses are available with blue or neutral flare coatings.

  • Pavo single lenses: from $2,299 (regular price $3,399)
  • Pavo 3-lens sets: from $5,499 (regular price $8,999), which is the 38.89% discount
  • Pavo 6-lens set: from $10,339 (regular price $14,999)

The lowest prices are for the neutral coating with imperial scales. Other coating and scale versions cost more, so check the configuration in the store.

Macro and probe lenses

The X-tract 18-28mm T8 is a parfocal full-frame probe zoom with up to 2.1:1 magnification. It is available in 0° (direct view), 90° (periscope), and 360° versions. The 90° version has the 37.15% discount from the press release.

  • X-tract 18-28mm 90°: $2,199 (regular price $3,499)
  • X-tract 18-28mm 0°: $2,499 (regular price $3,499)
  • X-tract 18-28mm 360°: $2,899 (regular price $3,999)
  • X-tract 3-lens set (0°/90°/360°): $7,499 (regular price $9,599)

The Gnosis macro primes (24mm, 32mm, 65mm, and 90mm T2.8) cover VistaVision and reach magnifications from 1:1 to 1.5:1. Each lens costs $3,499 (regular price $4,499), and 3-lens sets start at $8,999 (regular price $11,999).

Zooms and Octopus adapters

In addition to the education kit, the full-frame Catta Ace and the Super 35 Tango zooms are also discounted:

  • Catta Ace 35-80mm or 70-135mm: $1,599 each (regular price $1,799)
  • Catta Ace 18-35mm: $1,999 (regular price $2,299)
  • Catta Ace 3-lens set: $4,299 (regular price $4,999)
  • Tango 18-90mm: $6,799 (regular price $7,799)
  • Tango 65-280mm: $8,799 (regular price $9,799)
  • Tango 2-lens set: $12,499 (regular price $14,499)

The first-generation Octopus adapters (PL to E or DX, and EF to E, RF, or L) cost $169 instead of $269. The Octopus II, which DZOFILM introduced in June 2026, is not part of the discount and stays at $199.

Instagram campaign for anamorphic tips

DZOFILM is also running an Instagram campaign asking anamorphic shooters to share the one tip they wish they had known from the start, for example a practical trick, a mistake they will not make again, or a lens pairing or comparison that surprised them. The first prize is one Pavo lens ($3,399), and the second prize is one Arcana lens ($1,099). All participants get an extra 5% off the Black Friday price of Arcana and Pavo lenses.

The campaign runs until November 26 and is open to shooters worldwide. Check out their Instagram here.

Price and availability

The DZOFILM Black Friday sale runs until December 3, 2026, in the DZOFILM official store and at participating DZOFILM dealers. All prices in this article are from DZOFILM’s US store; dealer prices and regional prices can be different. The Arcana 3-lens kit offer at $2,699 ends on December 1, 2026. B&H lists the Arcana 3-lens kit at $2,699, and the kit is also available at CVP.

Are you planning to buy cine lenses this Black Friday, and is the Arcana kit, the Arles Zoom, or one of the Vespid Prime 2 kits on your list? Have you already shot with DZOFILM anamorphics? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Tilta Black Friday Sale 2026 – Up to 50% Off Cages, Daily Flash Deals, Free Gifts and Accessories

entry.content:
Tilta’s Black Friday sale 2026 is live and runs until November 30. The Tilta online store takes up to 50% off select camera cages, matte boxes, rigs, accessories, and adds daily flash deals of up to 35% off starting November 25. Orders over $399 come with a gift; many cages and kits come with a free matching accessory, and the Nucleus-M II Ultimate Kit ships with two free NP-F550 batteries. Here is what is included and what the main deals cost.

The sale runs from November 19 to November 30, 2026, Pacific Time, on Tilta’s US store. It also includes 20% off the Khronos Core for iPhone 18, triple reward points, and lower free shipping thresholds. Discounts vary by product, so not every item reaches 50%.

Featured deals: up to 50% off

The largest discounts in Tilta’s featured deals apply to smaller rigs. The Full Camera Cage for DJI Osmo 360 is 50% off at $14.50 (regular $29), and the Camera Cage for DJI Osmo 360 Horizontal Mounting Kit costs $17.50 instead of $35. The Camera Cage for DJI Osmo Action 3 Basic Kit is 40% off at $29.40 (regular $49).

For FUJIFILM shooters, the Vintage Camera Cage for Fujifilm X-T50 Base Kit is 39% off at $21.24 (regular $35). During the sale, it comes with a free Leather Camera Case for Fujifilm X-T50 in green.Tilta Vintage Camera Cage for Fujifilm X-T50.

Nikon users can take 15% off the Tilta Portable Charging Station for EN-EL15C. With four 2400mAh EN-EL15C batteries, the kit costs $101.15 (regular $119). The version with two batteries costs $63.75 (regular $75).

Cages, matte boxes and lens control

Tilta’s “On sale now” collection lists the most popular Black Friday items. The Camera Cage for Sony FX5 Pro Kit costs $242.10 (regular $269), and the Full Camera Cage for Sony FX5 costs $89.10 (regular $99). We covered the launch of the FX5 cage in July and later the EVF Extension Kit for the Sony FX5, which is also on sale.

The Tilta Mirage Matte Box is 10% to 15% off. The basic version costs $107.10 (regular $119), the version with VND $332.10 (regular $369) and the version with VND and motor $509.15 (regular $599). The Mirage also comes with a choice of free accessories.

For focus pullers, the Nucleus-M II Wireless Lens Control System is 10% off. The Hand Wheel Kit costs $809.10 (regular $899), and the Ultimate Kit costs $1,349.10 (regular $1,499). The Ultimate Kit also comes with two free Tilta NP-F550 batteries (3500mAh). We tested the system in our Nucleus-M II review. The Nucleus Auto Focus Adapter (E to PL), which adds autofocus to manual PL lenses on Sony E-mount cameras, is listed from $359.10 to $539.10, depending on the kit.

Daily flash deals from November 25

From November 25 to November 30, Tilta releases one or two flash deals per day at 9:00 AM PT (18:00 CET). Each deal uses a coupon code that appears on the Black Friday sale page at that time. The deals run until midnight PT or until they sell out, and most are limited to five orders. Tilta says there are no rainchecks or backorders. The schedule is:

  • November 26: Advanced Ring Grip for DJI Ronin, $519.35 instead of $799 (35% off)
  • November 27: Tilta Boulder Camera Cart (cart only, gray), $1,049.25 instead of $1,399 (25% off)
  • November 27: Nucleus-M II Hand Wheel Kit, $520 instead of $800 (35% off, 10 orders)
  • November 28: Tilta Lightweight Shoulder Rig in black, $220.35 instead of $339 (35% off, 10 orders)
  • November 29: Camera Cage for Sony FX3/FX30 V2 Pro Kit in black, $194.35 instead of $299 (35% off)
  • November 29: Camera Cage for Sony FX5 Pro Kit in black, $174.85 instead of $269 (35% off)
  • November 30: Nucleus Auto Focus Adapter (E to PL) Base Kit, $259.35 instead of $399 (35% off)
  • November 30: Nucleus Auto Focus Adapter (E to PL) with Dual Nano II Motor, $389.35 instead of $599 (35% off)

Two of these deals bring prices below the levels before Tilta’s September increase. The Nucleus Auto Focus Adapter Base Kit went from $299 to $399 on September 1, so the Cyber Monday price of $259.35 is lower than the old price. The Boulder Camera Cart in gray went from $1,199 to $1,399, and the flash price of $1,049.25 is also below the old price. Note that the flash deal list gives $800 as the regular price of the Nucleus-M II Hand Wheel Kit, while the product page shows $899.

Free gift over $399 and free accessories

Orders with a subtotal over $399 qualify for one free gift. Customers choose it in the cart or at checkout from 12 accessories worth up to $23 each. The choices include the Tilta Mini Table Top Tripod, the Pocket V-Mount Battery Plate V2, a USB-C 65W Power Adapter, a 15mm Carbon Fiber Rod Set (8in / 20cm), an ARCA quick release baseplate, and a leather shoulder strap. According to Tilta, the tripod, the battery plate and the power adapter are the most popular choices so far.

Separately, many products come with a free matching accessory. The Camera Cage for Nikon ZR kits includes a free PL Mount Lens Adapter Support for Nikon ZR. We reported on that cage at its announcement. Cages for the Sony a7 IV come with an HDMI cable clamp, the Sony ZV-E1 cages with an Arca baseplate, and the Full Camera Cage for BMPCC 6K Pro/G2 with a 15mm rod holder. The cages for the Sony a1 II/a9 III include an ARCA bottom plate with cable passthrough. For the Sony FX3/FX30 V2, Canon EOS R5 Mark II and Canon EOS R5 C cages, buyers can choose from several accessories. The Tilta CT08 75mm Cine Fluid Head with Carbon Fiber Tripod Legs comes with a free ARCA Manfrotto Dual Quick Release Receiver Kit. We tested the Tilta tripods last year.

The latest addition to Tilta’s Khronos ecosystem, the Khronos Core for iPhone 18, is 20% off.
