The larger Khronos iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max Ultimate Kit is 10% off at $539.10 (regular $599). Earlier generations of the system are in our Khronos field review, and we also covered the Khronos Cine Optical Lens Adapter for PL and E-mount lenses.

Archive and open box deals

The sale also includes “The Archive,” which Tilta describes as final stock and last-chance deals, and a section of open box items. According to Tilta, some Archive items are more than 70% off, and they do not return once sold out. For example, the Side Power Handle Type I for F570 batteries costs $30.62 (regular $119). Open box items are final sale.

Shipping, rewards and other regions

Shipping is free on US and Canada orders over $49, and on orders over $199 to Europe, Asia and Mexico. Tilta says that some heavier items are excluded. Every order during the sale earns triple reward points.

Tilta’s EU store and UK store also show Black Friday prices, but the discounts are not always the same as in the US. For example, the Nucleus-M II Ultimate Kit costs €1,274.15 (regular €1,499) in the EU store and £1,019.15 (regular £1,199) in the UK store. The Full Camera Cage for DJI Osmo 360 is €14.50 and £11.50, and the Mirage Matte Box with VND is €313.65 and £273.70.

Availability

The Tilta Black Friday sale runs from November 19 to November 30, 2026, and ends at midnight Pacific Time on Cyber Monday (09:00 CET on December 1). All US prices above come from the Tilta US store on November 20, 2026. The flash deal prices apply only on their day and with the coupon code. More details are in Tilta’s Black Friday announcement.

Are you waiting for one of the flash deals, or is there a Tilta cage on your list this year? Which deal would you pick? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: NANLITE vela Series Launched – Compact 150W and 300W all-in-one Spotlights
entry.summary: NANLITE has announced its new vela series consisting of compact all-in-one LED spotlights in two sizes. The vela 150 and vela 300 each come in a bi-color (b) and a full-color (c) version, and all four lights have a Bowens mount and a built-in power supply. The 150W models can als
entry.content:
NANLITE has announced its new vela series consisting of compact all-in-one LED spotlights in two sizes. The vela 150 and vela 300 each come in a bi-color (b) and a full-color (c) version, and all four lights have a Bowens mount and a built-in power supply. The 150W models can also run from USB-C PD power, a battery grip, or a V-mount battery. Pre-orders are open in the US.

These lights are all-in-one, compact point sources for interviews, livestreams, product shots, and location work. Instead of the usual cylindrical monolight body, the lights use a flat, rounded box with the Bowens mount built into the front. Because the power supply sits inside the housing, one AC cable powers them. We have covered several of NANLITE’s Bowens mount spotlights before, from the FS-150B and FS-200B to the FS-300C and, most recently, the FC-1200B and FC-1200C. The vela models are much smaller, and they are priced well below those lights.

Two sizes, bi-color or full color

The vela 150b and vela 300b are bi-color fixtures with a range of 2,700K to 7,500K. The vela 150c and vela 300c use NANLITE’s Nebula C4 light engine, which the company also uses in the FC-1200C. They cover 2,400K to 12,000K with ±150 green/magenta adjustment and add an HSI mode (hue 0 to 360, saturation 0 to 100). The full-color models have 14 built-in effects, and the bi-color models have nine.

For color rendering, NANLITE gives an average CRI of 96, TLCI of 98, and TM-30 Rf of 95 for the bi-color models. The full-color models reach an average CRI of 95, TLCI of 94, and TM-30 Rf of 92, and all four have a TM-30 Rg of 100. Dimming goes from 0 to 100% in 1% steps. The housings are color-coded: the bi-color lights are light “Mint Blue”, and the full-color lights are dark “Serene Blue”.

vela 150b and 150c

The 150W models have a flat profile of 7cm / 2.76in, with a width of about 12cm / 4.7in, and they weigh 0.9kg / 1.98lb. The full housing measures 160.5 x 123.4 x 69mm / 6.32 x 4.86 x 2.72in. According to NANLITE, they are approximately 60% smaller and 60% lighter than traditional spotlights of the same power rating. The bare beam angle is 85° on the 150b and 60° on the 150c. A detachable 180° mounting bracket with a 5/8″ baby pin receiver attaches to a V-shaped slot on the back, which can also hold a V-mount battery. A 1/4″-20 thread takes the bracket or the battery grip.

Each 150W light ships with the FL-11CP Fresnel lens, a 3m / 9.8ft AC cable, and a carrying bag. The Fresnel lens weighs 188g / 6.6oz, zooms steplessly from 21° to 40° and comes with a clip-on diffuser. Bare, at 1m / 3.3ft and 5600K, NANLITE specifies 10,300 lux for the 150b and 9,750 lux for the 150c. With the Fresnel lens at 21°, these figures rise to 52,600 lux and 44,200 lux. At 40°, they are 21,400 lux and 19,700 lux.

Power options on the 150W models

Besides AC power (100 to 240V), the vela 150b and 150c accept USB-C PD 3.1 input from 12 to 28V. The light detects the available power and limits its maximum output to match. A 30W source gives 20% brightness, 45W gives 30%, 60 to 65W gives 40%, 100W gives 65%, and a source of more than 140W gives 90%. Full output is only available on AC.

For handheld or stand use without mains power, NANLITE offers the BT-BG-14.4V73 battery grip. It has a 73Wh battery, USB-C and DC outputs of up to 100W, and a 1/4″-20 screw to mount the light directly. NANLITE quotes up to 45 minutes of runtime at 65% brightness and a recharge time of about 42 minutes with a 100W PD charger. With the CB-DT-PD D-Tap to USB-C PD adapter cable, a 155Wh V-mount battery runs the light for about 1 hour 40 minutes at 65%.

vela 300b and 300c

The 300W models have a flat profile of 12cm / 4.72in, with a width of about 14cm / 5.5in, and weigh 2.23kg / 4.92lb, with a housing of 293.5 x 138 x 123.5mm / 11.56 x 5.43 x 4.86in. NANLITE says they are approximately 40% smaller and 30% lighter than traditional spotlights of the same power rating. They have a top handle and a 180° adjustable mounting bracket with a 5/8″ baby pin receiver. The bare beam angle is 75°, and a 40° reflector, a 3m / 9.8ft AC cable and a carrying bag are in the box. The 300W lights run on AC only (100 to 240V, 4A maximum). NANLITE lists no USB-C PD or battery option for them.NANLITE’s size comparison of the vela 150 and vela 300 models with a traditional spotlight.

At 1m / 3.3ft and 5600K, the bare 300b gives 25,350 lux and the bare 300c gives 18,680 lux. With the 40° reflector, NANLITE specifies 66,600 lux for the 300b and 52,200 lux for the 300c. At 3m / 9.8ft, the figures are 6,800 lux and 5,370 lux, and at 5m / 16.4ft, they are 2,454 lux and 1,953 lux. As with the 150W pair, the bi-color version has the higher output.

Control, cooling and modifiers

All four models have one knob, two buttons, and a 1.28-inch display on the back. NANLINK App 2.0 gives wireless control of multiple lights, synchronized group effects and firmware updates. NANLITE describes the cooling system as new for this series. A fan cools the lights, and its speed changes automatically with the temperature. NANLITE gives a noise level as low as 20dB(A) at low fan speed.

Because of the Bowens mount, the lights accept Bowens mount modifiers without an adapter. NANLITE names its PJ-BMCP-36 projection attachment, its Bowens mount reflectors and the Bowens mount versions of its Rapid softboxes. NANLITE has also introduced two small octagonal softboxes with a quick-lock speed ring for the series, the 30cm SB-O-30 and the 40cm SB-O-40.The PJ-BMCP-36 projection attachment and the SB-O-30 and SB-O-40

NANLITE also shows an optional frame that holds four vela 150 lights together as one array, for more output from a single position.

Current limitations

The vela 300b and 300c have no battery or USB-C PD input, so they need mains power or a generator. On the 150W models, PD power limits the output to between 20% and 90%, depending on the source, and the battery grip runs the light for up to 45 minutes at 65% brightness. NANLITE lists on-board and NANLINK App control only, with no DMX or CRMX. The full-color models offer CCT, HSI and effects, but NANLITE does not list a gel or RGBW mode.

Price and availability

In the US, NANLITE takes orders at introductory prices that are below the listed regular prices. The vela 150b costs $167 (regular price $209), the vela 150c costs $199 ($249), the vela 300b costs $239 ($299), and the vela 300c costs $279 ($349). The 2-Light Kits cost $295 for the 150b ($369) and $367 for the 150c ($459). The FL-11CP Fresnel lens costs $19.90 separately, the battery grip $89.90, the D-Tap cable $23.90, and the SB-O-30 and SB-O-40 softboxes $34.90 and $49.90. NANLITE gives the expected availability as “coming soon”.

entry.title: Hollyland Solidcom SE – 2.4GHz Full-Duplex Intercom for Crews of Up to Five + Black Friday Deal
entry.summary: Small crews rarely need a broadcast intercom, but the director, camera operator, and gaffer still need to talk to each other without pressing a button on a walkie-talkie. The Hollyland Solidcom SE Global Version is a 2.4GHz full-duplex headset system for teams of two to five peop
entry.content:
Small crews rarely need a broadcast intercom, but the director, camera operator, and gaffer still need to talk to each other without pressing a button on a walkie-talkie. The Hollyland Solidcom SE Global Version is a 2.4GHz full-duplex headset system for teams of two to five people, with dual-mic noise cancellation, detachable batteries, and a range of up to 350m (1,100ft). From November 19 to November 30, Hollyland is offering up to 33% off the system for Black Friday. Here is what the Solidcom SE does on set, how the kits differ, how the Global Version compares with the SE Pro, and where its limits are.

We have covered Hollyland’s intercom line for years, from our Solidcom M1 review to the Solidcom C1 Pro and the larger Solidcom H1. The Solidcom SE Global Version sits at the small-crew end of that range. In our guide on how to choose a wireless intercom system for film production, we looked at where systems like this fit into different production sizes and workflows. Hollyland also offers the 1.9GHz Solidcom SE Pro, which extends the range and supports larger teams, so we will look at where the two versions differ below.

The Solidcom SE Global Version operates in the 2.4GHz band with automatic frequency hopping and a line-of-sight range of up to 350m (1,100ft). Each headset weighs approximately 185.2g (6.53oz) with its battery and uses dual-microphone Environmental Noise Cancellation (ENC), rated at more than 20dB of noise reduction. One master headset supports up to four remotes, giving the system up to five users.

What full-duplex changes on a small set

The important difference between an intercom and a walkie-talkie is not simply wireless range. In full-duplex mode, everyone in the Solidcom SE system can talk and listen at the same time, more like a phone call than a radio conversation. There is no need to wait for a channel to clear before answering.

On a three-person shoot, for example, a director can speak to the camera operator and gaffer continuously while all three hear the same conversation. A five-headset kit could add an assistant and another camera or lighting crew member. Everyone remains in one group, however. There are no separate channels for camera, lighting, or other departments.

For crew members who only need to speak occasionally, the SE also supports Push-to-Talk. The microphone boom can be moved up to mute the headset, while a button switches between mute and talk with a single press.

The headsets arrive pre-paired, so a kit works out of the box. If another remote is added later, pairing is done by holding the volume + button on the master and remote headset until they connect.

Noise cancellation for communication, not monitoring

The dual-mic ENC system processes the microphone signal to reduce ambient noise around the speaker’s voice. Hollyland specifies more than 20dB of environmental noise reduction from all directions and a signal-to-noise ratio of 71dB (±2dB). The electret microphone handles more than 115dB SPL, while the frequency response is 150Hz to 7kHz.

That frequency range is designed around speech. The Solidcom SE is therefore a communication system rather than a headset for monitoring production sound.

Hollyland also uses an algorithm to reduce wind noise outdoors. The headsets are rated IPX4 for water resistance, which provides protection against splashing water but does not make them waterproof. The operating temperature is 0 to 45°C (32 to 113°F).

Will the batteries last through a shooting day?

Each headset runs on a detachable 770mAh (2.926Wh) Li-ion battery pack that charges in less than three hours. Every Global Version kit includes one battery per headset and a 6-slot charging base. Spare batteries are sold separately, and the headsets can also be powered over USB-C.

The remotes are rated for approximately 12 hours, which should cover many production days. The master is the one to watch. With four remote headsets connected, Hollyland rates it at approximately 10 hours.

On a long shooting day, a spare battery for the master is a sensible addition. Because the batteries are removable, swapping one is faster than putting the whole headset out of service to recharge it. USB-C charging also means a power bank can keep a headset running if no charged spare is nearby.

Earpiece mode and comfort

Not every crew member wants to wear a headset all day. The USB-C port accepts Hollyland’s USB-C to 3.5mm adapter, letting the Solidcom SE sit around the neck while the user listens through a separate 3.5mm earpiece. Hollyland notes that only its own adapter supports this, and it isn’t included in the kits. Communication still uses the headset microphone.

For comfort, Hollyland compares the headset weight to a smartphone. The ear pads and microphone cushions are replaceable, which is useful when crew members share headsets. Over-ear pads are also available separately.

Three kits and a clear crew-size limit

The Solidcom SE Global Version comes in three configurations. The 2S kit includes one master and one remote headset; the 4S kit has one master and three remotes; and the 5S kit includes one master and four remotes.

The 2S and 4S kits can be expanded with additional remote headsets, so a crew can start small and add users later without replacing the whole system. A two-person setup can therefore grow to four or five users as production needs change, while the 5S kit arrives ready for the maximum supported crew size.

For small productions, that covers a useful range of setups, from a director and camera operator to a five-person team with additional camera, lighting or production crew. The ceiling is five users, so productions that need larger teams or separate communication groups will need to move to a bigger intercom system.

The Solidcom SE Global Version is also not compatible with the Solidcom C1 or C1 Pro.

Current limitations

The 2.4GHz band is shared with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and many wireless video transmitters. Automatic frequency hopping helps the SE move away from interference, but a crowded set or trade show can still be a more difficult RF environment than an open location. The quoted 350m (1,100ft) range is also a line-of-sight figure, so walls, vehicles, and other obstacles can reduce the usable distance.

The other limits come from the size of the system itself: five users at most, one talk group, and no compatibility with Hollyland’s other intercom systems. For a corporate shoot, documentary unit, or small commercial crew, those restrictions may not matter.

How the Solidcom SE Global compares with the SE Pro

Hollyland sells a second system with almost the same name: the Solidcom SE Pro, which we covered at its launch in April 2025. Both systems use 770mAh batteries, a 150Hz to 7kHz frequency response, more than 20dB of environmental noise reduction, and headsets weighing approximately 185.2g (6.53oz). Both also support Hollyland’s USB-C to 3.5mm earpiece adapter. The two systems aren’t compatible, so keep that in mind if you plan to expand the system later.

The most important difference is the radio. The SE Global Version transmits in the 2.4GHz band, which it shares with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and many other devices on set. The SE Pro uses the 1.9GHz DECT band, which Hollyland says keeps it clear of interference from 2.4GHz devices. Both systems use automatic frequency hopping. The SE Pro also has a longer line-of-sight range of 400m (1,300ft), compared with 350m (1,100ft) for the SE.

The second difference is team size. The SE stops at five users. The SE Pro supports up to 11 users with additional remote headsets and the required firmware update, and Hollyland sells it in 2S, 4S, 5S, 6S, and 9S kits. However, a larger system shortens the master headset’s battery life. Hollyland rates the SE Pro master at more than 5 hours with five remotes and around 3 to 3.5 hours with ten remotes, while each remote runs for more than 10 hours. Each SE Pro kit includes two batteries per headset, while the SE includes one.

Handling is nearly identical on both systems. Both the SE and SE Pro have MUTE and PTT functions, and on both you control talking with the microphone boom. The protection is different: Hollyland describes the SE Pro as dust- and water-resistant, while it describes the SE as water-resistant only. Neither product page gives an IP rating. Hollyland also claims an upgraded algorithm with speech enhancement for the SE Pro.

Which one fits your crew?

The SE Pro costs more. Its 4S kit has a list price of $679, compared with $459 for the SE 4S kit, so a four-person SE Pro system costs $220 more before any discount. The Black Friday offer in this article applies to the SE.

For a crew of up to five people who work mostly on location, away from crowded Wi-Fi, the SE does the job at a lower price. The SE Pro makes more sense for six or more people, for events, studios and trade shows where the 2.4GHz band is busy, or when you need the extra range. Because the two systems cannot be mixed, the SE Pro is also the safer choice if your crew may grow past five people.

Black Friday deal, price and availability

Hollyland’s Black Friday offer for the Solidcom SE runs from November 19 to November 30, 2026, with up to 33% off. In the US, the Solidcom SE 2.4G 4S kit drops from $459 to $308 on Amazon US. In the UK, the same kit drops from £354.82 to £237.71 on Amazon UK. For full specifications, visit the Hollyland website.

Do you still coordinate your small-crew shoots on walkie-talkies, or has a full-duplex headset system become standard on your set? Would the five-user Solidcom SE Global Version cover your crew, or would you need the additional capacity of the SE Pro? Let us know in the comments below!
